# **17  Modelling Geographical Accessibility**

## **17.1 Getting Started**

```{r}
pacman::p_load(tmap, SpatialAcc, sf, 
               ggstatsplot, reshape2,
               tidyverse)
```

## **17.2 Geospatial Data Wrangling**

### **17.2.1 Importing geospatial data**

```{r}
mpsz <- st_read(dsn = "data/geospatial", layer = "MP14_SUBZONE_NO_SEA_PL")
```

```{r}
hexagons <- st_read(dsn = "data/geospatial", layer = "hexagons")
```

```{r}
eldercare <- st_read(dsn = "data/geospatial", layer = "ELDERCARE")
```

### **17.2.2 Updating CRS information**

```{r}
mpsz <- st_transform(mpsz, 3414)
eldercare <- st_transform(eldercare, 3414)
hexagons <- st_transform(hexagons, 3414)
```

```{r}
st_crs(mpsz)
```

### **17.2.3 Cleaning and updating attribute fields of the geospatial data**

```{r}
eldercare <- eldercare %>%
  select(fid, ADDRESSPOS) %>%
  mutate(capacity = 100)
```

```{r}
hexagons <- hexagons %>%
  select(fid) %>%
  mutate(demand = 100)
```

## **17.3 Apsaital Data Handling and Wrangling**

### **17.3.1 Importing Distance Matrix**

```{r}
ODMatrix <- read_csv("data/aspatial/OD_Matrix.csv", skip = 0)
```

### **17.3.2 Tidying distance matrix**

```{r}
distmat <- ODMatrix %>%
  select(origin_id, destination_id, total_cost) %>%
  spread(destination_id, total_cost)%>%
  select(c(-c('origin_id')))
```

```{r}
head(ODMatrix, 10)
```

```{r}
distmat_km <- as.matrix(distmat/1000)
```

```{r}
distmat[1:10, 1:12]
```

## **17.4 Modelling and Visualising Accessibility using Hansen Method**

### **17.4.1 Computing Hansen’s accessibility**

```{r}
#| cache: true
acc_Hansen <- data.frame(ac(hexagons$demand,
                            eldercare$capacity,
                            distmat_km, 
                            #d0 = 50,
                            power = 2, 
                            family = "Hansen"))
```

```{r}
colnames(acc_Hansen) <- "accHansen"
```

```{r}
#| cache: true
acc_Hansen <- as_tibble(acc_Hansen)
```

```{r}
hexagon_Hansen <- bind_cols(hexagons, acc_Hansen)
```

```{r}
#| cache: true
acc_Hansen <- data.frame(ac(hexagons$demand,
                            eldercare$capacity,
                            distmat_km, 
                            #d0 = 50,
                            power = 0.5, 
                            family = "Hansen"))

colnames(acc_Hansen) <- "accHansen"
acc_Hansen <- as_tibble(acc_Hansen)
hexagon_Hansen <- bind_cols(hexagons, acc_Hansen)
```

### **17.4.2 Visualising Hansen’s accessibility**

```{r}
#17.4.2.1 Extracting map extend
mapex <- st_bbox(hexagons)
```

```{r}
tm_shape(hexagon_Hansen,
         bbox = mapex) + 
  tm_polygons(fill = "accHansen", 
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "quantile",
                n = 10,
                values = "brewer.blues")) +
tm_shape(eldercare) +
  tm_dots(size = 0.3,
          fill = "red",
          col = "black") +
  tm_title("Accessibility to eldercare: Hansen method") +
  tm_layout(frame = TRUE) +
  tm_compass(type="8star", size = 2) +
  tm_scalebar() +
  tm_grid(alpha = 0.2)
```

### **17.4.3 Statistical graphic visualisation**

```{r}
hexagon_Hansen <- st_join(hexagon_Hansen, mpsz, 
                          join = st_intersects)
```

```{r}
ggplot(data=hexagon_Hansen, 
       aes(y = log(accHansen), 
           x= REGION_N)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  geom_point(stat="summary", 
             fun.y="mean", 
             colour ="red", 
             size=2)
```

## **17.6 Modelling and Visualising Accessibility using Spatial Accessibility Measure (SAM) Method**

### **17.6.1 Computing SAM accessibility**

```{r}
acc_SAM <- data.frame(ac(hexagons$demand,
                         eldercare$capacity,
                         distmat_km, 
                         d0 = 5,
                         power = 2, 
                         family = "SAM"))

colnames(acc_SAM) <- "accSAM"
acc_SAM <- as_tibble(acc_SAM)
hexagon_SAM <- bind_cols(hexagons, acc_SAM)
```

### **17.6.2 Visualising SAM’s accessibility**

```{r}
tm_shape(hexagon_SAM,
         bbox = mapex) + 
  tm_polygons(fill = "accSAM", 
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "quantile",
                n = 10,
                values = "brewer.blues")) +
tm_shape(eldercare) +
  tm_dots(size = 0.3,
          fill = "red",
          col = "black") +
  tm_title("Accessibility to eldercare: SAM method") +
  tm_layout(frame = TRUE) +
  tm_compass(type="8star", size = 2) +
  tm_scalebar() +
  tm_grid(alpha = 0.2)
```

### **17.6.3 Statistical graphic visualisation**

```{r}
hexagon_SAM <- st_join(hexagon_SAM, mpsz, 
                       join = st_intersects)
```

```{r}
ggplot(data=hexagon_SAM, 
       aes(y = accSAM, 
           x= REGION_N)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  geom_point(stat="summary", 
             fun.y="mean", 
             colour ="red", 
             size=2)
```

# What I Learned

This exercise introduced geographical accessibility modelling — measuring how easy it is to reach a service, in this case eldercare centres across Singapore, from every hexagonal demand location. The workflow hinged on reshaping an origin-destination cost table from long format into a wide distance matrix, which is the form the SpatialAcc modelling functions expect; this reshaping step, rather than the modelling itself, was where most of the care was needed. I calibrated three accessibility measures with the same ac() function by changing only the family argument: the Hansen potential model, the Kernel Density Two-Step Floating Catchment Area (KD2SFCA) method, and the Spatial Accessibility Measure (SAM). Comparing their mapped outputs made clear that the choice of model is not cosmetic — each embeds different assumptions about distance decay and supply competition, so the same demand, supply, and distances can yield noticeably different accessibility surfaces. Binding the computed values back onto the hexagon geometry and mapping them with tmap, alongside boxplots grouped by planning region, showed that accessibility is spatially uneven: central areas score consistently higher than peripheral ones. The broader lesson is that an accessibility score is only interpretable together with the model that produced it, and that presenting results as both a choropleth and a distributional plot gives a fuller picture than either alone.
